1058.title: What you think now
1058.hook: compare with what you wrote on day 759
1058.howItsDone: Some people who keep a journal of their practice reread old entries at the end of a season or a year, and write a short note on what they think now beside what they wrote then.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was my teachers: eight people in hard places, and one line written to one of them. Today one more teacher comes back: the person who wrote a dated page at the start of the block on death. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

A page with a date on it. Three or four lines, plain as a grocery list. On day seven hundred fifty-nine, the first day of the block on death, this path asked one question before any tradition got to speak: what do you think happens when we die? Not what you were taught. Not what you ought to say. Just what came up first, even if it was a shrug, or I don't know. Then you dated it and put it away. Since then this path has brought in Socrates and the Gita, the Buddha and the Gospels, and others besides. Today the page comes back out.
screen: `A PAGE WITH A DATE ON IT.` → `DAY 759: WHAT DO YOU THINK?` → `THE PAGE COMES BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: First, read it as if a friend wrote it. The person who wrote those lines was honest with what they had. There's no grade on that page, and there's no grade today. Read it slowly, the way you'd read a note someone left you on the kitchen table. Second, look for small changes, not big ones. A changed mind is rarely a conversion scene. More often it's a word you'd now cross out, a fear that sits a little quieter, a picture you've added, a certainty that's gone soft at the edges. Or a question you didn't have before. Those count. Third, a teacher on changing your mind. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor whose notebook this path has read, wrote in his Meditations that if anyone could show him he was thinking or acting wrongly, he would gladly change, because he was after the truth, and the truth never harmed anyone. The harm, he said, comes from staying in error and ignorance. For him, changing wasn't the failure. Staying in error was. Fourth, staying put is an answer too. Some people reread their page and find they still think the same thing, only more clearly, or more calmly. That isn't a failed year. A view that has met Socrates, the Upanishads, the Psalms and a year of living, and is still standing, is not the same view it was. It's been tested. So whatever you find on the page, changed or unchanged, today's job is simply to notice it, and to write it down beside the old lines.
screen: `READ IT AS IF A FRIEND WROTE IT.` · `LOOK FOR SMALL CHANGES.` · `MARCUS: I WILL GLADLY CHANGE.` · `STAYING PUT IS AN ANSWER TOO.` · then, large: `WHAT CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to write what changed. If you have the page from day seven hundred fifty-nine, set it in front of you. If you don't, try to remember what you thought back then, as best you can. Sit, and let the breath slow down. Then ask the same question again, plainly: what do I think happens when we die? Notice what comes up first. After the bell, write it under the old lines, and then one more line that begins: what changed is. If nothing changed, write that, and why. The bell holds the time.
What you think now. The old question asked again, after a year of other voices, and set beside your first answer. Today's word.
Your line: what changed. Keep the two pages together. Sometime today, if it feels right, tell one person one thing you think differently now, about anything at all. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: Still open
1059.hook: the questions this year didn't close
1059.howItsDone: Some people on many paths keep a written list of their unanswered questions and return to it at the end of a year, noticing which ones have changed rather than trying to close them.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was what changed: the old page on death, and the new lines written beside it. Some things moved. Today is for the things that didn't settle at all. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

Plenty of kitchens have one drawer for things that don't belong anywhere else. Rubber bands, a key nobody can identify, the instructions for something you no longer own. You don't throw the drawer out. You just know it's there. A year of great questions has a drawer like that too. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: some of what we asked got an answer you could hold. And some of it got a stack of answers that don't agree, or no answer at all. Today we open the drawer, on purpose, and leave it open.
screen: `A DRAWER FOR WHAT DOESN'T FIT.` → `SOME QUESTIONS DIDN'T SETTLE.` → `OPEN THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: First, the question even the gods doubted. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa finds himself at the house of Death, and asks what happens to a person after dying: some say he is, some say he is not. Death answers that even the gods were once in doubt about this, that it's subtle and hard to know, and offers him wealth, long life and land if he'll ask anything else. Nachiketa keeps his question. Some questions are worth more than every prize offered for dropping them. Second, the hymn that wonders. The Hymn of Creation in the Rig Veda asks how everything began, and ends by wondering whether even the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not know. A sacred text that leaves its own question open. Third, the brother who won't sign. In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan says he can't accept a final harmony bought with a child's suffering. His brother Alyosha, who believes, answers from his own faith, but he doesn't walk away, and the chapter doesn't settle it for either of them. The novel keeps them both at the table. Fourth, open is not empty. These traditions have answers, and people live whole lives inside them. On this path, the answers stay in their own homes, and the choosing stays with you. So a question still open at the end of the year isn't a gap in the work. It's a door you know the location of. Some people keep a short list of questions like this and look at it once a year. Not to close them. To see which ones have changed shape, which ones have gone quiet, and which ones still wake them at night.
screen: `NACHIKETA KEEPS HIS QUESTION.` · `THE HYMN THAT WONDERS IF ANYONE KNOWS.` · `IVAN WON'T SIGN.` · `OPEN IS NOT EMPTY.` · then, large: `STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a list. Sit, and let the year's six questions pass by one at a time: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Don't hurry. As each one passes, notice whether something in it still tugs. A why. A what if. A person you still can't make sense of. After the bell, write down the questions that are still open for you, as plainly as you can, one per line. Three is plenty. If you pray, you can bring the list into prayer. If you don't, just keep it somewhere you'll find it again. The bell holds the time.
Still open. The questions this year asked and didn't close: kept, named, and left on purpose with the door ajar. Today's word.
Your line: still open. When one of your open questions comes up today, don't rush to settle it. Say to yourself, still open, and let it stay. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: Ahead: thinkers and practices
1060.hook: year four reads the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson and Thoreau, and studies the science and schools of practice
1060.howItsDone: Some people who follow a reading path look over the coming year's books before they start, and pick one they are most curious about to give them something to look forward to.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was still open: a short list of questions the year didn't close. Keep it handy. Some of next year's company has been carrying questions like those for a very long time. Day one thousand sixty.

Next year's reading list is short enough to tape to the fridge. On it: a small old book of short chapters from China, a Frenchman writing about himself, and two Americans from the same town, one giving lectures, one building a cabin by a pond. Below them, a stack of studies on what quiet attention does to a person, and a long row of doors marked Zen, Sufi, Jewish, Christian contemplative, Sikh, and more. That's the list for year four. This year asked six great questions in many voices. Next year changes the shape: fewer voices, read slowly, and then the practice itself, looked at closely. Today, a look at what's ahead.
screen: `A READING LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `FEWER VOICES, READ SLOWLY.` → `WHAT'S AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the Tao Te Ching, chapter by chapter. It's a short Chinese classic, some chapters only a few lines long, and it keeps praising what most people overlook. Water, it says, does good to everything and settles in the low places nobody wants. The empty space inside a bowl is what makes the bowl useful. Year four walks through it slowly, one chapter at a time. Second, Montaigne. In his note to the reader at the front of his Essays, Montaigne says that he himself is the matter of his book. No grand subject: one man, his habits, his moods, his fears, looked at honestly. He tries out a thought, turns it over, and isn't embarrassed to change his mind. Third, Emerson and Thoreau. Emerson, in his essay Self-Reliance, wrote: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." His friend Thoreau went off to live by Walden Pond, and wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." One wrote about trusting the inner voice; the other went to the pond to try living by his. Fourth, the science and the schools. After the thinkers, year four studies what researchers can honestly say about attention, habit and compassion, including what the studies don't show. Then it visits the world's schools of practice, each in its own home: Zen and Theravada, Tibetan Buddhism, Christian contemplatives, Jewish, Muslim and Sufi, Hindu, Sikh and Chinese ways, and modern secular ones. And at the end, how to choose a practice, and how to respect the ones you don't choose. Year three asked what life is for. Year four asks how people have actually trained themselves to live it.
screen: `THE TAO TE CHING, ONE CHAPTER AT A TIME.` · `MONTAIGNE: I AM THE MATTER OF MY BOOK.` · `EMERSON TRUSTS; THOREAU TESTS.` · `THE SCIENCE, AND THE SCHOOLS.` · then, large: `THE THINKERS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to pick one thing to look forward to. Sit, and let the list go past slowly: the old Chinese book, the Frenchman, the lecturer, the man at the pond, the studies, the schools. Don't choose with your head yet. Notice which one your attention leans toward, the way you lean toward a window when someone says look. When the bell ends, name it, out loud or on paper. If nothing leans, that's fine too: the first chapter begins either way. The bell holds the time.
Ahead. Year four: the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson and Thoreau, then the science of practice and the world's schools of practice. Today's word.
Your line: the thinkers. Today, tell one person which of next year's thinkers you're curious about, and why, even if the why is only a hunch. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: Year three close
1061.hook: a year of great questions, answered in many voices
1061.howItsDone: Some people mark the end of a year of study by rereading their notes and choosing one question to carry into the next year, sitting with it quietly rather than trying to settle it.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was the thinkers: the old Chinese book, the Frenchman, the lecturer and the man by the pond, waiting next year. They can wait one more day. Today the year of great questions closes. Day one thousand sixty-one.

Gently. Live, then. Love is the practice. Work well, then rest. Let it go. Smaller, and glad. Those were the lines that closed each block this year, one for each great question: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Read them in a row and they sound almost like a life. None of them is an answer to the question it closed. Each one is more like a way of carrying it. And that is where year three ends: not with a verdict, but with a way of holding what's still unsolved.
screen: `GENTLY. LIVE, THEN. LOVE IS THE PRACTICE.` → `WORK WELL, THEN REST. LET IT GO. SMALLER, AND GLAD.` → `A WAY OF CARRYING IT.`

segments.voice: First, many voices, kept apart. On suffering, the Buddha named suffering and its cause, Job argued, and Julian heard that all shall be well. On death, the Gita spoke of worn clothes, the Gospels of resurrection, Socrates of two possibilities, without claiming to know which was true. They didn't agree, and this year never pretended they did. Each answer stayed in its own home, in its own words. Second, two pictures from a letter. A few days ago we heard Rilke tell a young poet to love the questions themselves. In that same letter he gives two images for what those questions are like: locked rooms, and books written in a language you can't read yet. You don't break a locked door down, and you don't force a foreign book to make sense. You live near them. Perhaps, Rilke says, one day you'll find you've lived your way into an answer. Third, loving a question isn't the same as solving it. A question you love is one you keep near the way you keep a friend near: you return to it, you notice it has changed, you don't need it to end. Nachiketa loved his so much he turned down Death's gifts for it. Fourth, why this is a close and not a stop. Tomorrow a new year begins, and the questions come with you. A question carried into new company tends to sound different there, the way a familiar song does in a new room. That's what this year was for: not a shelf of finished answers, but a handful of questions you know well enough to love.
screen: `MANY VOICES, KEPT APART.` · `RILKE: LOCKED ROOMS, FOREIGN BOOKS.` · `LOVING A QUESTION, NOT SOLVING IT.` · `A CLOSE, NOT A STOP.` · then, large: `LOVE THE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with one question you love. Look at the list you made two days ago, or just let the year's questions pass by until one stays. Choose the one you're most glad to still be asking. Settle, and hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a warm cup. Don't try to answer it. When your mind starts building an answer, set the answer down and come back to the question. If you pray, you can carry the question into prayer. If you don't, let it simply keep you company. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. A year of great questions, suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, answered in many voices and kept open with care. Today's word.
Your line: love the questions. Write your question somewhere you'll see it as year four begins, and ask it once more tonight, without needing an answer. Day one thousand sixty-one.
